title: The Annunciation (25 March)
hookLine: nine months before Christmas, the Word takes flesh

lines: WHITE IN THE MIDDLE OF LENT.
cards: Count back nine months from December 25 and you land on March 25. So in the middle of Lent, with purple on the altar and Easter still weeks off, there's a sudden white solemnity: Christmas, seen from the beginning.

By old custom, church bells rang three times a day, at dawn, at noon and at dusk, and people working in the fields stopped and bowed their heads to remember this exact moment. Some churches still ring them.

teach.b: Luke sets it in Nazareth, a town in Galilee. The angel Gabriel comes to a young woman betrothed to Joseph and greets her: hail, full of grace.
He tells her she will conceive a son, and call him Jesus, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. Mary doesn't simply nod.

She asks a real question, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" The angel answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the power of the Most High will overshadow her.
He tells her that her old cousin Elizabeth, called barren, is six months pregnant.
"Because no word shall be impossible with God." And then Mary's answer, the hinge of the story: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
In Latin, the first word of that last phrase is fiat, let it be done, and Catholics often call this Mary's fiat. It's not passive. She asked, she listened, and she chose.
Christians believe that in that moment the Word, who in John's gospel was there in the beginning, took flesh in her.
That's why, at Mass today, people kneel at the words of the Creed about the incarnation, as they do on Christmas. And that's what the bells were for.

teach.h: BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: The Angelus, rung morning, noon and evening, walks through this scene in three short lines with a Hail Mary after each: the angel's message, Mary's be it done, and the Word made flesh.
A whole Christmas, three times a day, small enough to say in a field.

how: Catholics keep March 25 as the Solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord (moved when it falls in Holy Week or the Easter octave), kneel at the Creed's words on the incarnation; the Angelus is traditionally prayed at 6 a.m., noon and 6 p.m.

games.q: you're Mary. the angel has answered your question: the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and no word is impossible with God. what do you say?
o: give me time to ask Joseph.
behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me.
I'm not worthy; choose someone else.
games.why: be it done to me according to thy word. her fiat, given after a real question.

practice: If you pray and know it, pray the Angelus now: three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary. If not, let its shape guide you: first breath, a message arrives; second breath, a question is asked; third breath, a yes is given.
Then hold something you've been asked to carry that you didn't plan, and ask whether a yes is possible.

wordCard.voice: The Annunciation. The angel Gabriel's message to Mary, and her yes, kept on March 25, nine months before Christmas. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: let it be done, the first word of Mary's answer in the Vulgate (Luke 1:38).

carryVoice: Your line: be it done. Christmas is nine months away from here. See you tomorrow.
